home.name: The Milky Way
home.constellation: Visible all around us; the core lies towards Sagittarius
home.distance: We are about 26,000 light-years from the galactic centre
home.discovery: Known since prehistory; resolved into stars by Galileo in 1610
home.summary: The Milky Way is the barred spiral galaxy that contains the Sun, the Solar System and every star you can see with the unaided eye. Its disc is wrapped in spiral arms of gas, dust and young stars, and the Sun sits in a minor arm — the Orion Spur — roughly two thirds of the way out from the centre.
highlights: A supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, of about 4.3 million solar masses sits at the centre.
The Sun takes roughly 225–250 million years to complete one orbit of the galactic centre.
From a dark site the galactic plane appears as a milky band split by the Great Rift, a lane of interstellar dust.
The Milky Way and Andromeda are approaching each other and will begin merging in about 4.5 billion years.

galaxies.name: Andromeda Galaxy
galaxies.summary: The largest galaxy in the Local Group and the most distant object most people can see without a telescope. It is closing on the Milky Way at about 110 km/s and the two will merge in roughly 4.5 billion years.

image.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a bright spiral seen at an angle with dark dust lanes and two companion galaxies.

galaxies.name: Triangulum Galaxy
galaxies.magnitude: 5.7 — a naked-eye challenge under dark skies
galaxies.summary: The third-largest member of the Local Group, a face-on spiral rich in star-forming regions including NGC 604, one of the largest known stellar nurseries.

image.file: VST snaps a very detailed view of the Triangulum Galaxy.jpg
image.alt: The Triangulum Galaxy seen face-on, with loosely wound blue spiral arms and pink nebulae.

galaxies.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
galaxies.magnitude: 0.9 — obvious to the unaided eye from the south
galaxies.summary: The Milky Way's most prominent satellite galaxy and home to the Tarantula Nebula, the most active star-forming region known in the Local Group. Supernova 1987A exploded here.

image.alt: The Large Magellanic Cloud, a bright irregular smudge of stars with a central bar.

galaxies.name: Small Magellanic Cloud
galaxies.summary: A dwarf companion to the Milky Way, tidally distorted by its larger neighbour. Studies of its Cepheid variables gave Henrietta Leavitt the period–luminosity law used to measure the universe.

image.alt: The Small Magellanic Cloud, an elongated cloud of stars beside the globular cluster 47 Tucanae.

galaxies.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
galaxies.summary: The first galaxy recognised as a spiral, in 1845. Its textbook arms are being wound up by an ongoing interaction with the small companion NGC 5195.

image.alt: The Whirlpool Galaxy, a face-on spiral with a smaller yellow companion galaxy at the end of one arm.
image.credit: NASA, ESA, S. Beckwith (STScI) and the Hubble Heritage Team

galaxies.name: Sombrero Galaxy
galaxies.summary: Seen almost exactly edge-on, its brilliant bulge is cut by a sharp dust lane that gives the galaxy its hat-like shape. It hosts a billion-solar-mass central black hole.

image.alt: The Sombrero Galaxy, a glowing bulge crossed by a dark, sharply defined dust lane.
image.credit: NASA/ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

galaxies.name: Pinwheel Galaxy
galaxies.summary: A lopsided giant spiral nearly twice the size of the Milky Way, packed with bright H II regions and a frequent host of supernovae.

image.alt: The Pinwheel Galaxy seen face-on, with blue spiral arms studded with pink star-forming regions.
image.credit: NASA, ESA, K. Kuntz (JHU) and the Hubble Heritage Team

galaxies.name: Cigar Galaxy
galaxies.summary: A starburst galaxy forming stars ten times faster than the Milky Way after a close encounter with M81, driving a superwind of hot gas out of its disc.

image.alt: The Cigar Galaxy seen edge-on, with red filaments of gas blasting out perpendicular to its disc.
image.credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

galaxies.name: Centaurus A
galaxies.summary: The closest active galactic nucleus, most likely the remnant of a merger. Relativistic jets from its central black hole make it one of the brightest radio sources in the sky.

image.alt: Centaurus A, a bright elliptical galaxy crossed by a thick, warped band of dark dust.

galaxies.name: Messier 87
galaxies.summary: A monster elliptical at the heart of the Virgo Cluster with trillions of stars and 12,000 globular clusters. Its black hole, M87*, was the first ever imaged, in 2019.

image.alt: Messier 87, a featureless glowing elliptical galaxy with a thin jet emerging from its core.
image.credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

galaxies.name: Sculptor Galaxy
galaxies.summary: One of the brightest galaxies beyond the Local Group and the dustiest starburst spiral nearby, easily seen from southern latitudes in binoculars.

image.file: The Sculptor Galaxy in a new light.jpg
image.alt: The Sculptor Galaxy, a dusty spiral tilted at a steep angle with a bright core.

galaxies.name: Bode's Galaxy
galaxies.summary: A near-perfect spiral and the dominant galaxy of its group. Its gravitational tug on neighbouring M82 triggered that galaxy's starburst.

image.alt: Bode's Galaxy, a symmetric spiral with tightly wound arms and a bright yellow core.
image.credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

galaxies.name: Antennae Galaxies
galaxies.diameter: About 500,000 light-years including the tidal tails
galaxies.summary: Two spiral galaxies caught mid-collision. Tidal forces have flung out long streams of stars — the 'antennae' — while the crash triggers explosive star formation.

image.alt: The Antennae Galaxies, two merging galaxies glowing with blue star clusters and red gas.
image.credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

galaxies.name: IC 1101
galaxies.diameter: Up to 4 million light-years including its diffuse halo
galaxies.summary: One of the largest galaxies known: a diffuse cD elliptical at the centre of a rich cluster, grown huge by swallowing its neighbours over billions of years.

image.alt: The galaxy cluster Abell 2029 with the supergiant elliptical galaxy IC 1101 at its centre.

galaxies.name: Hubble Ultra-Deep Field
galaxies.type: Thousands of galaxies in one view
galaxies.diameter: A patch of sky about a tenth the width of the full Moon
galaxies.summary: A long exposure of an apparently empty patch of sky that revealed roughly 10,000 galaxies, some seen as they were only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

image.file: Hubble ultra deep field high rez edit1.jpg
image.alt: A dark field scattered with thousands of galaxies of every shape, size and colour.
image.credit: NASA, ESA and S. Beckwith (STScI) and the HUDF Team
